title: Audit Trail
blurb: Five ways an organization checks its own security — a scan, a test, an audit, a review, and a log check. Sort each scene into the assessment that produced it, or the one that's still missing.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.15 (Security Assessment and Testing) · CISSP April-2024 outline 6.1, 6.2, 6.5
hint: Ask two questions: did anyone try to actually exploit anything, and is the output a technical finding or a formal opinion against a standard? That sorts most of the board.
note: Several scenes describe a report or a claim that already exists but is missing a specific piece of proof. Sort those to the assessment type that would have produced the missing proof, not the one that produced the claim in front of you.

zones.name: Vulnerability scan
zones.def: An automated, repeatable probe of hosts, ports and configurations against known-weakness databases (missing patches, misconfigurations, exposed services) that stops at identification — it never attempts to exploit what it finds. A credentialed run, logged in with an authorized scanning account (usually one with administrative or root-level rights so it can read patch levels and local settings), sees deeper than an unauthenticated one, but neither one proves a flaw is actually reachable by an attacker; that proof belongs to a penetration test.

zones.name: Penetration test
zones.def: Authorized, scoped testing under agreed Rules of Engagement where testers actively attempt to exploit weaknesses — white-box (source and internal detail given), gray-box (partial knowledge), or black-box (none) — to prove real-world impact. It goes past a vulnerability scan's list of findings into actually using one, and its final deliverable is a report, not a live compromise left running.

zones.name: Audit
zones.def: A structured review of controls against a defined standard, regulation, internal policy or baseline, producing a documented opinion rather than a list of technical flaws. It may be internal (the organization's own staff checking adherence to its own policy), external, or third-party (for example an ISO 27001 certification audit, a PCI DSS assessment or a SOC attestation). An auditor evaluates and recommends but never decides or remediates on the organization's behalf. For SOC 1 and SOC 2 reports specifically, a Type I opinion covers the system description and the design of controls as of a single date, while a Type II also tests that those controls operated effectively across a period, typically six to twelve months.

zones.name: Code review
zones.def: Static, pre-production inspection of an application's own source — by a peer developer or an automated static-analysis tool — for defects before the code ever runs. It catches what only exists in the text of the code itself, such as a hardcoded secret, which a scan or test that only observes the running application would never see.

zones.name: Log review
zones.def: Retrospective inspection of events already recorded by systems and security tools (SIEM, NetFlow, admin activity logs) to confirm what actually happened and who actually touched what — reconstructing history from a passive record, never by probing or exploiting the live system in the moment.

items.label: An automated tool sweeps 200 hosts on a subnet overnight against a known-CVE database and returns a list of twelve machines running unpatched software, without ever attempting to leverage any of the flaws it flags.
items.why: Automated identification that stops short of exploitation is the defining boundary; a penetration test would be the tempting neighbor once someone actually tries to use one of these twelve flaws, but nobody here does.

items.label: The same scanning tool is re-run against a finance server, this time logged in with an authorized local-admin scanning account instead of anonymously, and the new report surfaces internal misconfigurations the earlier run never saw.
items.why: This is a credentialed scan going deeper because it can see past the front door — still identification, not exploitation, so it stays here rather than sliding into a penetration test just because a login was used.

items.label: A report from an automated tool lists open ports, guessed operating systems, and a handful of stale services running across a subnet, generated overnight entirely without logging into any host or attempting to leverage what it finds.
items.why: Automated identification of ports, OS fingerprints and stale services — all without any exploitation attempt — is exactly what an unauthenticated vulnerability scan produces. A penetration test is the tempting neighbor once someone actually tries to use one of those stale services, but nothing here goes past enumeration.

items.label: Before deciding what deeper testing a new subnet needs, a team just wants a fast, repeatable inventory of every live host and open port on it.
items.why: Establishing what exists on the network is the network-discovery flavor of scanning, and it normally comes first — a penetration test's information-gathering phase builds on this baseline rather than replacing it.

items.label: A vulnerability report rates a flaw in Meridian Retail's checkout API at CVSS 9.8, but leadership won't fund an emergency fix until someone shows an attacker could actually reach cardholder data through it.
items.why: A severity score describes potential impact, not proven reachability; only an authorized attempt to actually exploit the flaw supplies the missing proof, which a scan — by design — never attempts.

items.label: Testers are handed Meridian Retail's source code and internal network diagrams up front, letting them skip most reconnaissance and go straight at logic flaws in the loyalty-points module.
items.why: Full prior knowledge makes this a white-box, known-environment test; the tempting confusion is gray-box, but gray-box gives only partial knowledge — full source and diagrams go all the way to white-box.

items.label: Before any tester touches Meridian Retail's network, legal, IT security, and senior management all sign off on a rules-of-engagement document naming exactly which systems are off-limits.
items.why: The planning phase and its Rules of Engagement are what make active exploitation lawful and scoped; skipping this multi-party sign-off is what turns testing into unauthorized intrusion, so its presence is the tell for this assessment type.

items.label: After finding a SQL injection flaw in a returns portal, a tester pulls a small sample of customer records to prove the flaw is real, then destroys the copy and reports the finding.
items.why: Actually using the flaw to extract data, however briefly, is the exploitation step that separates this from a vulnerability scan, which would have flagged the injection point and stopped there.

items.label: A firm hires an outside team and tells them nothing beyond Meridian Retail's public domain name, wanting the engagement to mirror what an external attacker would actually see.
items.why: Zero prior information is the black-box, unknown-environment form — the trap is assuming any testing without full access must be an audit, but this is still active exploitation attempted from an outsider's starting point, which audits never do.

items.label: A payments processor asks a vendor for a report confirming that its access controls, encryption, and monitoring didn't just exist on paper but actually functioned correctly every day for the past twelve months.
items.why: Confirming operating effectiveness over an extended period is a SOC 2 Type II opinion; a Type I report would only cover whether the controls were well-designed at a single point in time, which is the weaker, tempting-but-wrong read of 'confirming controls.'

items.label: A hospital hires a CPA firm with no financial or reporting relationship to the hospital to render an independent opinion on whether its safeguards meet a healthcare regulation's requirements.
items.why: Independence from the org being reviewed, plus a documented opinion against a named regulation, is what makes this an audit rather than an internal security assessment, which the hospital's own staff could run without any outside opinion at all.

items.label: A marketing team wants a short, public document to reassure customers that a new SaaS product's controls are sound enough to post on the company website.
items.why: This is a SOC 3 report — the public, management-assertion-level cousin of SOC 2, intentionally light on technical detail; expecting it to carry SOC 2's confidential, control-by-control detail is the trap, since that level stays under NDA.

items.label: Reviewing an incident afterward, a committee notes that the auditor who assessed Meridian Retail's controls last quarter also personally ordered the remediation team to change its firewall rules.
items.why: An auditor's role is to evaluate and recommend, never to decide or act on the organization's behalf; an auditor directing a remediation crosses into a role this assessment type structurally excludes, which is the finding worth flagging.

items.label: A small private company, without the budget for an outside firm, has its own compliance staff check password-policy adherence purely for internal management's use, against no published external standard.
items.why: This is still an audit — an internal, informal one — because it is a compliance check against a defined policy; it only stops being an audit if nobody is checking against any standard or baseline at all, which is not the case here.

items.label: Before a payment module merges, two developers who did not write it walk through the code line by line looking for logic and security defects, without running the application at all.
items.why: Inspecting the source itself, by someone other than its author, with the app never executed, is a static review; the moment someone actually runs the module to see how it behaves, it becomes a different, dynamic form of testing.

items.label: Before any change to Meridian Retail's encryption library ships, the team follows a fixed six-stage process — planning, overview, preparation, inspection, rework, follow-up — with formal entry and exit criteria at each stage.
items.why: This is a Fagan inspection, the most formal variant of this assessment type; its rigidity distinguishes it from an informal peer walkthrough, but both stay in the same zone because both examine the code itself rather than the running system.

items.label: An automated static-analysis tool scans a repository's raw source without compiling or executing it, and flags a hardcoded database password sitting in a configuration file.
items.why: Finding a secret embedded in text nobody runs is a static-analysis result; a dynamic scanner exercising the live application for weeks would never trip this finding, since the running app never displays the raw source line containing it.

items.label: A dynamic scanner has exercised Meridian Retail's live checkout service for weeks and found nothing wrong, yet a hardcoded database password sits untouched in a source file no human or static tool has ever opened.
items.why: The missing evidence is a look at the code itself: dynamic testing only observes what the running application does, so a secret that the application never displays back to a tester stays invisible until someone actually inspects the source.

items.label: A junior developer's pull request to a permissions module sits unmerged for a week because no policy requires a second person to look at it before it ships.
items.why: The gap here is the missing second set of eyes on the code itself before release; a later vulnerability scan or penetration test could eventually catch a resulting flaw, but only after the flawed code is already live, which defeats the point of catching it pre-production.

items.label: Every quarter, a security manager samples admin-account activity across Meridian Retail's production servers to confirm privileged users haven't touched files outside their duties.
items.why: Sampling already-recorded activity for misuse is a retrospective check on history, not a live probe of the system — a penetration test would be the tempting neighbor, but nothing here is being actively attacked or exploited.

items.label: All of Meridian Retail's servers sync their clocks to a common time source before their events feed into a central console, so an investigator can trust the order in which two systems recorded the same incident.
items.why: Synchronized timestamps are what make this assessment type's core output — a trustworthy sequence of events — usable at all; without it, an investigator reconstructing what happened couldn't rely on the record, even though the events were still captured.

items.label: Investigators determine exactly which employee copied a sensitive file at 2:14 a.m. entirely from records already stored in the SIEM, without touching the live system at all.
items.why: Reconstructing an event purely from a passive, already-captured record is this assessment type's signature move; a penetration test only produces new evidence by acting on a live system, which is the opposite of what happens here.

items.label: A retained NetFlow record from a border firewall lets the team determine that an internal host quietly talked to a suspicious external address three weeks before anyone noticed.
items.why: This is a review of a passively retained record after the fact; a vulnerability scan run today would find whatever weaknesses exist now, but it can't tell the team what already happened three weeks ago.

items.label: A signed audit opinion states that Meridian Retail's access controls are well designed, but nobody can show which specific privileged accounts actually touched the finance database last month.
items.why: An audit opinion can confirm a control is well designed without ever confirming what day-to-day activity actually occurred under it; only a review of the recorded access events themselves supplies proof of who actually touched what.
